title: Fill the same tank
hook: Hydrogen beats petrol kilogram for kilogram. Now fill the same tank with each.

knows: that burning a fuel releases energy (pay-first-then-profit)
that a gas takes far more room than a liquid (one-ml-of-steam)
doesNotKnow: that "energy per kilogram" and "energy per litre" can rank fuels in opposite orders
that hydrogen wins one and loses the other by a factor of thousands

misconception: Hydrogen is simply the best fuel, so a tank of it holds more energy than the same tank of petrol.
objective: The learner can say that hydrogen carries about 3 times petrol's energy per kilogram but, as gas at room pressure, about 2,900 times less per litre (about 3.4 times less even liquefied), and explain that the gas is so light per litre.

claims.text: Burning hydrogen to liquid water releases about 286 kJ/mol, about 142 MJ per kilogram (stage label 'hydrogen: 142 MJ/kg' and readout 'Per kg: H₂ · petrol 142 MJ · 48 MJ'; reveal: 'about 142 MJ'; hook: 'Hydrogen beats petrol kilogram for kilogram'; question: 'about 3 times').
claims.source: ΔfH(H2O, l) = −285.83 kJ/mol (CODATA Key Values for Thermodynamics, 1989; CRC Handbook) / molar mass of H2 2.016 g/mol (IUPAC 2021) = 141.8 MJ/kg (node, demo-builder 2026-10-14). Demo.tsx H2_J_KG. Brief claim 1.
claims.note: Opened: CRC 'Standard Thermodynamic Properties' table as transcribed in the PyPI package chemicals 1.5.2 (H2O(l) -285.8), JANAF 1998 in the same package (-285.830) and ATcT 1.112 (-285.825). CODATA itself not opened; the -285.83 figure agrees with all three. H atomic weight 1.00794 (chemicals elements table) gives 2.016. Node: 285.83/2.016 = 141.78 MJ/kg, shown as 142 MJ.

claims.text: Burning octane (standing in for petrol) releases about 5,470 kJ/mol, about 48 MJ per kilogram; both heats are higher heating values, water formed as liquid (stage label 'petrol (octane): 48 MJ/kg'; reveal: '48 MJ for petrol'). The higher-heating-value convention is not shown on the stage.
claims.source: 8(−393.51) + 9(−285.83) − (−250.1) = −5,470.5 kJ/mol: ΔfH CO2(g) −393.51 and H2O(l) −285.83 kJ/mol (CODATA), ΔfH n-octane(l) −250.1 kJ/mol (CRC, Standard thermodynamic properties of chemical substances); / 114.23 g/mol = 47.9 MJ/kg (node). Cross-check: CRC heat of combustion of n-octane about −5,470 kJ/mol. Ratio to hydrogen 141.8 / 47.9 = 2.96 (stage '×3.0' not shown; question 'about 3 times'). Brief claim 2.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-840, 2026-10-14): the stage footnote 'octane for petrol · water formed as liquid' was removed (learner r10: noise for a beginner); the label 'petrol (octane)' stays; previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. Earlier note: Opened: CRC table (n-octane(l) -250.1, CO2 -393.5, H2O(l) -285.8) and JANAF/ATcT (CO2 -393.522/-393.474, octane(l) -249.73). Node: 8(393.51) + 9(285.83) - 250.1 = 5,470.4 kJ/mol (5,470.1 to 5,470.9 across the tables); / 114.232 g/mol = 47.89 MJ/kg, shown as 48 MJ. 'Petrol' is a disclosed stand-in ('octane for petrol' on the stage). From the same CRC table, the common petrol hydrocarbons (C5-C8 alkanes, toluene, xylene) give 42-49 MJ/kg. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Re-check after the stage footnote was removed. PyPI chemicals 1.5.2 formation enthalpies: n-octane(l) CRC -250.1 (ATcT -249.73, WebBook -250.29), CO2(g) -393.52 (JANAF), H2O(l) -285.83 kJ/mol: 8(-393.52) + 9(-285.83) + 250.1 = -5,470.5 kJ/mol; / 114.229 g/mol = 47.89 MJ/kg ('48 MJ/kg'). Both are higher heating values (liquid water). The label 'petrol (octane)' still discloses the stand-in; the HHV convention is in the claim, not on the stage, which the claim says.

claims.text: Hydrogen gas at 25 °C and 1 atm has a density of about 0.082 g/L, so a litre of it carries about 12 kJ (0.012 MJ) when burned (reveal: 'a litre of hydrogen gas at room pressure weighs only 0.08 g, so it carries about 12 kJ (0.012 MJ, the hairline)'; stage label 'hydrogen gas: 0.012 MJ/L (12 kJ), a hairline'; on the stage's linear 0-35 MJ axis its bar is drawn at the 1.5 px minimum).
claims.source: Ideal gas law ρ = PM/RT = 101,325 × 0.002016 / (8.314 × 298.15) = 0.0824 kg/m³ = 0.0824 g/L; hydrogen is close to ideal at 1 atm. × 141.8 MJ/kg = 11.7 kJ/L (node). Demo.tsx RHO_H2_GAS, H2_GAS_J_L. Brief claim 3. Builder node re-run 2026-10-14: 141.78 MJ/kg x 8.24e-5 kg/L = 11,684 J/L = 0.0117 MJ/L; octane 47.89 MJ/kg x 0.703 = 33.67 MJ/L; ratio 2,881.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-840, 2026-10-14): stage now uses a linear axis and writes the hydrogen-gas figure in MJ too (learner r10); previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. Earlier note: Derivation re-run: PM/RT = 0.0824 g/L, x 141.78 MJ/kg = 11.68 kJ/L ('12 kJ', '0.08 g'). 'Close to ideal' checked against the CRC second virial coefficient of H2 at 298 K (+15.4 cm3/mol, chemicals 1.5.2): Z = 1.0006 at 1 atm. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Ideal gas: rho = 101,325 x 2.01588e-3 / (8.314462618 x 298.15) = 0.0824 g/L; x 141.79 MJ/kg (HHV from the same chemicals tables: 285.83 kJ/mol / 2.01588 g/mol) = 11.68 kJ/L = 0.012 MJ/L. 'Close to ideal' as in the previous pass (Z = 1.0006). The new linear-axis label 'hydrogen gas: 0.012 MJ/L (12 kJ), a hairline' and the reveal ('0.08 g', 'about 12 kJ (0.012 MJ, the hairline)') match.

claims.text: Octane's density is about 0.70 kg/L (so about 34 MJ per litre burned) and liquid hydrogen's about 71 g/L at its boiling point, about −253 °C (so about 10 MJ per litre) (stage labels 'petrol (octane): 34 MJ/L', 'liquid hydrogen: 10 MJ/L', button 'Liquefy hydrogen (−253 °C)'; reveal: 'a litre of petrol carries about 34 MJ', 'liquefied at −253 °C').
claims.source: CRC Handbook: physical constants of organic compounds (n-octane 0.703 g/cm³ at 20 °C) and properties of cryogenic fluids (para-hydrogen liquid density about 70.8 kg/m³ at the normal boiling point 20.3 K = −252.9 °C). 47.9 MJ/kg × 0.703 = 33.7 MJ/L; 141.8 × 0.0708 = 10.0 MJ/L (node). Assumption disclosed on the stage caption: octane stands in for petrol, a mixture with a similar energy per kilogram. Brief claim 4.
claims.note: The CRC organic-constants and cryogenic tables named in the source were not opened. Checked instead against tables I did open in chemicals 1.5.2: the Perry/DIPPR-105 liquid-density fits give n-octane 0.707 kg/L at 20 °C and 0.703 at 25 °C ('about 0.70'), and liquid H2 70.6 kg/m3 at 20.39 K ('about 71 g/L'). The CRC heat-of-vaporization table gives H2's normal boiling point as 20.39 K = -252.8 °C ('about -253 °C'). Node: 33.67 MJ/L and 10.04 MJ/L.

claims.text: Per litre, octane carries about 2,900 times the energy of hydrogen gas at 1 atm and about 3.4 times that of liquid hydrogen (readout 'Per litre: petrol ahead gas ×2,900 · liquid ×3.4'; reveal: 'it lost by about 2,900 times', 'hydrogen holds about 3.4 times less per litre'; right option 'about 3,000 times less').
claims.source: 33.67 MJ/L / 11.68 kJ/L = 2,882 (two significant figures 2,900; nearest option 3,000); 33.67 / 10.04 = 3.35 (3.4) (node, from claims 1-4). Demo.tsx ratio().
claims.note: Derivation re-run: 33.67 MJ / 11.68 kJ = 2,881 (shown as x2,900; nearest option 3,000) and 33.67 / 10.04 = 3.35 (x3.4). The formatting functions (sig2, ratio, joules) give exactly the strings on the stage and in the reveal. With any petrol hydrocarbon from c2 (30-37 MJ/L) the ratio is 2,600-3,200, so the answer holds.

claims.text: Which fuel is 'best' depends on whether you are short of mass or short of space (reveal).
claims.source: Follows from claims 1-5: the per-kilogram and per-litre rankings are opposite. A framing sentence, not a claim about vehicles or tanks; the lesson makes no claim about 700-bar tanks (brief, Differs from).
claims.note: Derivation from c1-c5: the per-kg and per-litre rankings are opposite. Framing only; no claim about vehicles is made.

recall.question: A drone must carry the most energy for the least weight; a ship's fuel tank has a fixed volume. Which unit should each designer compare fuels by?
options: Drone by energy per kilogram, ship by energy per litre
recall.why: Energy per kilogram and energy per litre can rank fuels in opposite orders: hydrogen gas wins per kilogram by about 3 times and loses per litre by thousands. Short of mass, compare per kilogram; short of space, per litre.
